225.title: Barabbas (Mark 15:1–15)
225.hook: the crowd chooses a rebel over Jesus
225.howItsDone: On Palm Sunday and Good Friday many churches read the passion aloud with the congregation speaking the crowd's lines, so that everyone says crucify him and remembers that the crowd's failure can be anyone's.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a rooster crowed twice in a courtyard, Peter, and your line was he wept.

You've watched a pile-on. A comment section, a group chat, a hallway. One person says something, a few join in, and within minutes a whole crowd is certain. Nobody quite remembers how it started, and nobody wants to be the one who says, wait. Early in the morning, the council binds Jesus and hands him over to Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor, because only Rome can carry out an execution. Pilate asks him: are you the King of the Jews? Jesus answers, thou sayest it, then goes silent again, and Pilate marvels. Outside, a crowd is gathering.
screen: `A PILE-ON.` → `HANDED OVER TO PILATE.` → `A CROWD GATHERS.`

segments.voice: Mark says that at the feast the governor used to release one prisoner, whoever the people asked for. No record outside the Gospels mentions this custom, and historians aren't sure how it worked. In prison is a man called Barabbas, held with rebels who had committed murder in an uprising. Pilate asks the crowd: will you have me release the King of the Jews? He knew, Mark adds, that the chief priests had handed Jesus over out of envy. And the chief priests stir up the crowd to ask for Barabbas instead. Now look at the name. Barabbas is Aramaic: bar abba, son of the father. Remember abba, from the garden, four days ago? Jesus called God abba. So the crowd is offered two men: one called son of the father, and one Christians call the Son of the Father. Some old copies of Matthew's Gospel even give the rebel's first name as Jesus. What then shall I do with him? Pilate asks. Crucify him, they shout. Why, what evil hath he done? They shout louder. And in the King James Bible: "And so Pilate, willing to content the people, released Barabbas unto them, and delivered Jesus, when he had scourged him, to be crucified." Willing to content the people. The most powerful man in the province does what the loudest voices want. That morning's crowd, stirred up by a few, was wrong. And many Christians see one more thing here: the guilty man walks free, and the innocent one takes his place.

segments.voice: Picture a crowd you've seen lately turn on someone, online, at work, in the news: the people in it, one by one, ordinary people caught up in the noise, and the one they're shouting at. If you pray, you can pray for both, the crowd and the person in the middle; if you don't, simply wish them all a quieter heart.
Barabbas. Bar abba, son of the father: the rebel the crowd chose to set free instead of Jesus.
Your line: the crowd isn't always right. Someone has to be the one who says, wait. See you tomorrow.

226.title: The crown of thorns (Mark 15:16–32)
226.hook: soldiers mock; Simon of Cyrene carries the cross; passers-by jeer
226.howItsDone: Some Christians, especially Catholics and Anglicans, walk the Stations of the Cross, especially on Fridays in Lent, stopping to remember moments like the crown of thorns and Simon of Cyrene carrying the cross.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Barabbas went free, and your line was the crowd isn't always right.

The soldiers lead Jesus into the governor's courtyard and call together the whole company. Then they put on a show. They dress him in purple, twist a crown out of thorns and press it on his head. They salute him: hail, King of the Jews! They strike his head with a reed, spit on him, and kneel in mock worship. It's the kind of cruelty bored, powerful people invent when someone can't fight back. Then they strip off the purple, put his own clothes back on him, and lead him out to crucify him.
screen: `THE WHOLE COMPANY, CALLED TOGETHER.` → `PURPLE, AND A CROWN OF THORNS.` → `HAIL, KING OF THE JEWS.`

segments.voice: On the road out of the city, the soldiers grab a man coming in from the country, Simon of Cyrene, and make him carry the cross. Mark adds a detail nobody needed: Simon was the father of Alexander and Rufus. Why name the sons? Mark doesn't say; some readers think his first audience knew the family. A stranger pressed into service, and his name kept. They come to Golgotha, which Mark translates: the place of a skull. They offer him wine mixed with myrrh, and he doesn't take it. They crucify him and divide his clothes by casting lots. Above his head, the charge: the King of the Jews. Two bandits are crucified with him, one on each side. Then the mocking starts again, from everyone. People walking past shake their heads: you who would destroy the temple, save yourself! The chief priests and scribes say to each other, in the King James Bible: "He saved others; himself he cannot save." Even the men crucified beside him join in. The strange thing is that the mockers keep saying things that, to Mark's readers, are true. They call him king in mockery; Christians call him king. They say he saved others; Mark has spent the whole gospel showing just that: a leper, a little girl, a man in the tombs. And himself he cannot save is, for Christians, close to the whole point. As Christians tell it, he doesn't come down, not because he can't, but because saving others is what he's doing. The mockers get the words right and the meaning upside down.

segments.voice: Think of someone who's the butt of the joke right now, a kid at school, a coworker everyone rolls their eyes at, a stranger online, and picture their face. Then picture Simon, who happened to be walking by and ended up carrying the weight, and what walking alongside that person might look like: one kind word, one seat next to them. If you pray, you can hold them before God.

227.title: Why have you forsaken me? (Mark 15:33–41)
227.hook: he cries the first line of Psalm 22, and a Roman soldier says: truly the Son of God; the women watch
227.howItsDone: Some churches hold a service on Good Friday afternoon, around the ninth hour, and some pray Psalm 22 or meditate on the last words of Jesus from all four Gospels.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a crown of thorns and a crowd of mockers, Golgotha, and your line was he saved others.

Some of the hardest words anyone says are said at a hospital bedside, at 3am, when no answer comes. Why? Where are you? Mark doesn't soften what happens next. At the sixth hour, around noon, darkness covers the whole land until the ninth hour, about three in the afternoon. Then Jesus cries out with a loud voice. Mark gives the words in Aramaic, then translates them. They are the only words from the cross that Mark records.
screen: `DARKNESS AT NOON.` → `THE NINTH HOUR.` → `A LOUD CRY.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani? which is, being interpreted, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" Those words weren't new: they're the opening line of Psalm 22. The psalm starts in anguish: surrounded, mocked, bones out of joint, enemies dividing his garments. It ends in trust, the psalmist praising God in the great congregation. Christians read the cry in different ways, and the readings sit together. Some hear real abandonment, the Son going all the way down into the silence people feel when God seems gone. Others suggest that naming a psalm's first line can call up the whole psalm, so he may be praying all of Psalm 22, ending included. Some hold both. Either way, it matters that the prayer of the dying Jesus is a question. Some bystanders say: he's calling Elijah! One runs to give him sour wine on a sponge. Then Jesus gives a loud cry and breathes his last. At that moment, Mark says, the curtain of the temple is torn in two, from top to bottom. And the Roman centurion standing facing him, the soldier in charge of the execution, says: "Truly this man was the Son of God." Mark's gospel, in the King James text, opens by calling Jesus the Son of God. Now, at the cross, the one who says it out loud is not a disciple but a Roman soldier. And watching from a distance: the women. Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joses, Salome, and many others who had followed him from Galilee. The disciples had fled. The women stayed.
screen: `ELOI, ELOI, LAMA SABACHTHANI?` · `THE FIRST LINE OF PSALM 22.` · `THE CURTAIN TORN, TOP TO BOTTOM.` · `THE WOMEN WATCHED.` · then, large: `TRULY THIS MAN WAS THE SON OF GOD.`

segments.voice: If you can, open Psalm 22 in any Bible and read it slowly, all the way through, noticing where it's darkest and where it turns. If you can't, sit with its first line, my God, my God, why, and think of someone asking that question right now. You don't need an answer for them; the women didn't have one either, they just stayed.
Eloi, Aramaic for my God, the first word of Jesus's cry from the cross. The opening line of Psalm 22, cried aloud in anguish and trust.
Your line: the women stayed. When words run out, staying can still say something. Until tomorrow.

228.title: Joseph of Arimathea (Mark 15:42–47)
228.hook: a council member boldly asks for the body and lays it in a tomb
228.howItsDone: On Holy Saturday some churches keep a quiet day of waiting by the tomb; in Orthodox churches an embroidered cloth showing the burial is carried in procession, and Joseph of Arimathea is honored with a feast day in several churches.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a cry from the cross, Eloi, the first line of Psalm 22, and your line was the women stayed.

When someone dies, somebody has to do the practical things. Call the family. Sign the forms. Pick the clothes. It's an unglamorous kindness, and sometimes a brave one. It's evening on the day before the Sabbath. Jesus is dead. The disciples are gone. The law in Deuteronomy says a hanged body must not stay up all night, but this body is in Roman hands. Somebody has to ask for him. And the man who does is someone Mark has never mentioned before.
screen: `EVENING, THE DAY BEFORE THE SABBATH.` → `A BODY IN ROMAN HANDS.` → `SOMEBODY HAS TO ASK.`

segments.voice: Mark introduces him in one breath, in the King James Bible: "Joseph of Arimathaea, an honourable counsellor, which also waited for the kingdom of God, came, and went in boldly unto Pilate, and craved the body of Jesus." A counsellor: a member of the council, the same council that just condemned Jesus. Mark earlier said all of them condemned him; Luke adds that Joseph had not agreed with their decision. Honorable, Mark calls him, and waiting for the kingdom of God, the kingdom Jesus announced in Mark's first chapter. Then the verb. He went in boldly: the Greek word means he dared. Walking into the Roman governor's house to ask for the body of a man just executed as king of the Jews could cost him his standing, maybe more. He goes anyway. Pilate is surprised Jesus is already dead, calls the centurion to confirm it, and gives Joseph the body. Joseph buys fine linen, takes him down, wraps him, lays him in a tomb cut out of the rock, and rolls a stone against the door. Two people are watching: Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses. They see where he is laid, and that detail matters for Sunday. The disciples, who knew him best, are nowhere. The one who shows up is an insider Mark hasn't mentioned before. Several churches keep a feast day for him. Sometimes courage is loud. Sometimes it's a respectable man asking an awkward question, then doing the heavy lifting himself.

segments.voice: Think of someone who has died, a grandparent, a friend, someone you barely knew, and ask what kindness you could still do for them: visiting their grave, calling the person they left behind, telling their story to someone who never met them. Pick the one that feels a little awkward, the one that takes a bit of daring. If you pray, you can remember them before God.

229.title: Trembling and astonishment (Mark 16:1–8)
229.hook: the women find the tomb empty; the oldest copies end with them fleeing, afraid
229.howItsDone: Christians celebrate the resurrection at Easter and on Sundays; some churches hold sunrise services on Easter morning, and Orthodox Christians greet each other with Christ is risen, answered, truly he is risen.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a council member who dared to ask for the body, Joseph, and your line was he went in boldly.

The Sabbath is over. Very early on Sunday, as the sun comes up, three women walk to the tomb: Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome. They've bought spices to anoint his body, the last thing they can do for him. On the way they worry about something very practical: who will roll away the stone for us? Mark says it was very great. Two of them had seen where he was laid. Then they look up. The stone is already rolled back.
screen: `VERY EARLY, THE FIRST DAY OF THE WEEK.` → `WHO WILL ROLL AWAY THE STONE?` → `IT'S ALREADY ROLLED BACK.`

segments.voice: They go into the tomb, and sitting on the right side is a young man in a long white robe. They are terrified. He says, in the King James Bible: "Be not affrighted: Ye seek Jesus of Nazareth, which was crucified: he is risen; he is not here: behold the place where they laid him." Then a message: go, tell his disciples, and Peter, that he goes before you into Galilee; there you will see him, as he said. And Peter. Of all the names to single out, the one who denied him three times by the fire. Then comes the last verse of Mark in the oldest complete copies: "And they went out quickly, and fled from the sepulchre; for they trembled and were amazed: neither said they any thing to any man; for they were afraid." That's it. No appearance of the risen Jesus. No reunion. Just women running from an empty tomb, shaking. In Greek the sentence ends, literally, they were afraid, for: on a small word, gar, like a sentence cut off mid-breath. Scholars still argue about it. Maybe the last page was lost. Maybe Mark meant to stop here. If he did, the ending is a kind of invitation: the story isn't finished; it hands the next step to whoever is reading. And the women can't have stayed silent forever, or there'd be no story to read. Mark leaves them in trembling and astonishment: not calm, not neat, but awe. Trembling is tromos; astonishment is ekstasis, a word for being beside yourself, something so big it takes a person outside themselves.
screen: `A YOUNG MAN IN A WHITE ROBE.` · `TELL HIS DISCIPLES, AND PETER.` · `THEY WERE AFRAID, FOR.` · `TROMOS AND EKSTASIS.` · then, large: `HE IS RISEN; HE IS NOT HERE.`

segments.voice: Think of something in your life that ended, a job, a friendship, a season, a home, and remember what the women carried on that walk: the heaviness, the practical worries, who will roll away the stone. Then ask gently what began after that ending, even if you didn't see it at the time; you don't need a neat answer. If you pray, you can hold that ending before God.
Ekstasis, Greek for astonishment, being beside yourself. What seized the women at the empty tomb, paired with tromos, trembling.
Your line: he goes before you. The stone was rolled back before they arrived. Two hundred twenty-nine days now.

230.title: The longer ending (Mark 16:9–20)
230.hook: later verses add appearances and a commission; scholars note it wasn't in the earliest manuscripts
230.howItsDone: The longer ending is read in Catholic and Orthodox services, often around the Ascension, and many Protestant Bibles print it with a note that the earliest manuscripts end at verse eight.

segments.voice: Yesterday, an empty tomb and women who fled in trembling and ekstasis. Your line was he goes before you.

Open a Bible to the end of Mark and you might notice something odd. After verse eight, many modern Bibles put in a line, a bracket, or a small note: some of the earliest manuscripts end here. Then they keep going. Twelve more verses. If yesterday's ending left you hanging, the women running and afraid, you're in good company. Very early on, Christians felt that too, and the church ended up with more than one way to finish the story.
screen: `A BRACKET AFTER VERSE EIGHT.` → `SOME MANUSCRIPTS END HERE.` → `TWELVE MORE VERSES.`

segments.voice: Here's what the longer ending says. The risen Jesus appears first to Mary Magdalene, out of whom he had cast seven devils. She tells the mourning disciples, and they don't believe her. He appears to two of them walking in the country; they tell the rest, and again nobody believes. Then he appears to the eleven at a meal and scolds them for their unbelief and hardness of heart. And he gives them their commission, in the King James Bible: "Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature." Then he is taken up into heaven, and they go out and preach everywhere. Now the honest part. The two oldest complete Greek manuscripts of Mark, from the three hundreds, stop at verse eight. These twelve verses differ from the rest of Mark in vocabulary and style, and they sound like a summary of appearances told in the other Gospels and Acts. So most scholars think a later hand added them. Some manuscripts even have a second, shorter ending, just a sentence or two. But the longer ending is also very old. A church writer named Irenaeus seems to quote it well before the year two hundred, and it's in the vast majority of manuscripts. Churches hold it in different ways. The Catholic and Orthodox churches receive it as part of scripture and read it in their services. Many Protestant Bibles print it with a note. Almost everyone agrees on what it's doing: finishing the thought. Fear becomes a mission. The disciples who fled are sent out into all the world.
screen: `MARY MAGDALENE, FIRST.` · `THEY DID NOT BELIEVE.` · `NOT IN THE OLDEST COPIES.` · `CHURCHES HOLD IT IN DIFFERENT WAYS.` · then, large: `GO YE INTO ALL THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: If you can, open Mark 16 and read verses one to eight slowly, then stop and notice how it feels to end on they were afraid. Then read verses nine to twenty and notice how it feels to end on a mission; you don't have to decide anything about manuscripts. If you pray, you can offer both, the fear and the going, to God.

Irenaeus, the early church writer who quotes Mark's longer ending well before the year two hundred. Appearances, a commission and an ascension, missing from the oldest copies and very old all the same.
Your line: go into all the world. Two endings: one afraid, one sent out. Day two hundred thirty, done.

231.title: Camp 4 close: back to Galilee
231.hook: the young man said: he's going ahead of you to Galilee, back where it all began (Mark 16:7)
231.howItsDone: Churches that follow a lectionary read through one Gospel across a year of Sundays; in the three-year cycle shared by Catholics and a number of Protestant churches, Mark is the Gospel of the second year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Irenaeus and the longer ending; your line was go into all the world. Now the end of the week, and the close of camp four.

Have you ever gone back to your hometown after something big happened? The streets are the same. The diner is the same. You're not. At the empty tomb, the young man in white gave the women a message for the disciples. In the King James Bible: "he goeth before you into Galilee: there shall ye see him, as he said unto you." Not to Rome. Not to the temple. Back to Galilee: the lake, the boats, the nets, the little towns where it all began.
screen: `BACK TO YOUR HOMETOWN.` → `HE GOETH BEFORE YOU INTO GALILEE.` → `WHERE IT ALL BEGAN.`

segments.voice: For seventy-five days, this camp has read Mark's Gospel in order, a few verses at a time. It began with a single line: the beginning of the good news. Then the heavens torn open, and fishermen told to leave the nets. Friends dug through a roof. A leper heard I am willing. A sower threw seed everywhere, and Jesus slept on a cushion in a storm. A little girl heard talitha koum, get up. Five thousand were fed, and a woman told she was a dog answered back, and her daughter was healed. At Caesarea Philippi came the question at the center of the book: who do you say I am? Then the road to Jerusalem: take up your cross; a blind man named Bartimaeus asked to see; a widow gave all she had. And in these last days of the camp: perfume poured out, bread broken, abba in the garden, Peter weeping by the fire, a crown of thorns, the women who stayed, and an empty tomb. Mark's ending sends the disciples back to the beginning. Some readers think Mark wants his readers, too, to go back to chapter one and read it again, knowing how it ends. The disciples misunderstood again and again the first time through. Read again, the same stories look different. The very first verse, in the King James Bible: "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God." The beginning, as if the whole book is only the start. Tomorrow a new camp begins, camp five, the depths, opening with Jesus sitting down on a mountain to teach.
screen: `SEVENTY-FIVE DAYS OF MARK.` · `FROM THE NETS TO THE EMPTY TOMB.` · `BACK TO GALILEE, BACK TO CHAPTER ONE.` · `CAMP FIVE: THE DEPTHS.` · then, large: `THE BEGINNING OF THE GOSPEL.`

segments.voice: Open a Bible, if you can, to the first verse of Mark and read it slowly, the way you'd now, after everything, noticing which word lands differently; if you can't, say it quietly to yourself. Then let the one story from this camp that stays with you most come up on its own. If you pray, you can give thanks for it.
Beginning. The very first word of Mark, and where its ending sends you back, now knowing how it ends.
Your line: start again, knowing more. The end of Mark points back to its first line. Camp four, complete.
